title: Prompt Caching
summary: An agent re-sends the same system prompt and tool definitions on every loop iteration, paying to recompute them each time. Prompt caching stores the model's computed prefix so repeated tokens are billed at a steep discount and processed faster. The catch: caches match on an exact, unchanging prefix, so you must order the message so everything static comes first and anything variable comes last. Providers differ — some cache automatically, others require you to mark the cache point explicitly.

subtopics.title: What prompt caching actually reuses
subtopics.explanation: When a model processes your prompt it computes an internal representation of every token before generating. Prompt caching saves that computed prefix so a later call with the same leading tokens skips the recompute and is billed at a fraction of the normal input rate. It reuses computation, not answers — the model still generates fresh output. This is the mechanism that makes an agent's repeated system prompt and tools nearly free after the first call.
subtopics.example:
# conceptually, the model 'reads' tokens left to right and caches the prefix
system = "You are a support agent. Rules: ..."   # identical every call
tools = "[get_order, issue_refund, ...]"           # identical every call

# first call: full price to compute + store the prefix
# later calls with the SAME leading tokens: prefix is reused cheaply
prefix = system + tools
print("cacheable prefix length (chars):", len(prefix))
# caching reuses the COMPUTED prefix, not the model's answer

subtopics.title: Design a stable prefix: static first, variable last
subtopics.explanation: A cache only hits if the leading tokens are byte-for-byte identical to a prior call, so the golden rule is to put everything that never changes — system instructions, tool schemas, long reference docs — at the very front, and anything that varies — the user's turn, timestamps, retrieved snippets — at the end. Even one changed character early on invalidates the whole cached prefix. Ordering messages this way is the single design decision that determines whether caching helps at all.
subtopics.example:
def build_messages(user_input: str):
    return [
        # ---- STATIC PREFIX (cacheable) ----
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_RULES},   # never changes
        {"role": "system", "content": TOOL_SCHEMAS},   # never changes
        # ---- VARIABLE SUFFIX (not cacheable) ----
        {"role": "user", "content": user_input},       # changes each call
    ]

# BAD: a timestamp at the top would bust the cache every single call
# {"role": "system", "content": f"Now: {datetime.now()} ..."}
print([m["role"] for m in build_messages("where is order A-1?")])
# static content FIRST is what makes the prefix reusable

subtopics.title: Cache hits vs misses
subtopics.explanation: A cache hit means the model found a stored prefix matching your leading tokens and billed those at the discounted rate; a miss means it computed (and possibly stored) the prefix at full price. The first call is always a miss that primes the cache, and entries expire after a short idle window, so a cold or bursty workload sees more misses. Understanding the hit/miss distinction tells you when caching will and won't pay off.
subtopics.example:
cache = {}  # maps prefix -> already computed

def process(prefix, full_rate=0.003, cached_rate=0.0003):
    if prefix in cache:              # HIT: cheap
        return cached_rate, "hit"
    cache[prefix] = True             # MISS: pay full, then store
    return full_rate, "miss"

print(process("SYS+TOOLS"))  # (0.003, 'miss')  first call primes it
print(process("SYS+TOOLS"))  # (0.0003, 'hit')  now discounted
# the first call always misses; repeats hit until the entry expires

subtopics.title: Provider differences: explicit vs automatic
subtopics.explanation: Providers implement caching differently. Some (e.g. Anthropic-style) are explicit: you mark where the cacheable prefix ends with a cache_control breakpoint on a message, and you control what gets stored. Others (e.g. OpenAI-style) are automatic: long identical prefixes are cached for you with no flag, though you get less control. Either way the stable-prefix rule holds — but knowing whether your provider needs an explicit marker decides whether you must change your request code.
subtopics.example:
# EXPLICIT (Anthropic-style): mark the end of the cacheable prefix
explicit = {
    "role": "system",
    "content": SYSTEM_RULES + TOOL_SCHEMAS,
    "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},  # <- you set the breakpoint
}

# AUTOMATIC (OpenAI-style): no flag; identical long prefixes are cached for you
automatic = {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_RULES + TOOL_SCHEMAS}

print("cache_control" in explicit)   # True  -> you opt in
print("cache_control" in automatic)  # False -> provider handles it
# same stable-prefix rule; different opt-in mechanics per provider

subtopics.title: The savings math
subtopics.explanation: Cached input tokens are billed at a large discount (often ~10% of the normal input rate), so the more of your prompt that is a stable, reused prefix, the bigger the saving — and in an agent loop that re-sends the same system+tools every step, the prefix is most of the input. You compute the saving by splitting input into cached vs fresh tokens and pricing each part. Doing this math is how you prove caching is worth the extra request complexity before adopting it.
subtopics.example:
IN_RATE = 0.003
CACHED_RATE = 0.0003   # ~10% of full input rate

def input_cost(cached_tokens, fresh_tokens):
    return (cached_tokens/1000)*CACHED_RATE + (fresh_tokens/1000)*IN_RATE

# a step: 4000-token static prefix (cached) + 500-token fresh user turn
with_cache = input_cost(cached_tokens=4000, fresh_tokens=500)
no_cache   = input_cost(cached_tokens=0,    fresh_tokens=4500)
print(round(with_cache, 5), round(no_cache, 5))  # 0.0027 0.0135
# the bigger the reused prefix, the larger the saving per step

foundations.overview: Prompt caching is a provider feature that stores the model's computed representation of a prompt prefix so later calls with the same leading tokens skip recomputation, billing those tokens at a steep discount (often around 10% of the normal input rate) and processing them faster. It reuses computation, not answers — the model still generates fresh output every time. The mechanism is prefix-based: a cache hit requires the leading tokens to be byte-for-byte identical to a prior call, so the essential design move is to order your request with everything static (system rules, tool schemas, long reference material) at the very front and everything variable (the user's turn, timestamps, retrieved context) at the end. One changed character early on invalidates the whole cached prefix. The first call is always a miss that primes the cache, and entries expire after a short idle window. Providers differ in mechanics — some require an explicit cache_control breakpoint, others cache long identical prefixes automatically — but the stable-prefix rule is universal. For agents, where the same system prompt and tools are re-sent every loop iteration, caching turns the largest, most repetitive part of the input nearly free, which you confirm with a simple before/after cost calculation.
foundations.formalDefinition: Prompt caching stores the model's precomputed key/value representation of a message prefix keyed by that prefix's exact tokens; a subsequent request whose leading tokens match the stored prefix incurs a cache hit and bills those tokens at a reduced cached rate, while any divergence in the prefix causes a miss billed at the full input rate. Effective use requires arranging messages so all static content precedes all variable content, optionally marking the cache boundary explicitly where the provider requires it.
foundations.whyItMatters: An agent re-sends its system prompt and tool definitions — often thousands of tokens — on every single loop iteration, and those tokens dominate input cost. Prompt caching bills that repeated prefix at a fraction of the rate, cutting the cost and latency of the most repetitive part of an agentic workload without changing behavior, which is one of the highest-leverage, lowest-risk optimizations available.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the model as a reader who must read your document from the top every time before writing a reply. Caching lets it keep a bookmark: if the opening pages are identical to last time, it jumps to the bookmark and only reads the new pages at the end. So you write the unchanging chapters first and put anything that changes after the bookmark — change one word in the early chapters and the reader has to start over from page one.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Caching immutable system prompts and tool schemas across every step of an agent loop, reusing a large fixed context (a policy document, a long code file, a knowledge base chunk) across many user questions, keeping few-shot examples in a cached prefix, and serving high-traffic assistants where thousands of requests share the same instructions.
foundations.performanceImpact: Cached prefix tokens are billed at a large discount and are also faster to process (the model skips recomputing them), so caching reduces both per-call cost and time-to-first-token; the benefit scales with the ratio of stable prefix to fresh suffix, which in a typical agent loop is high because system+tools repeat every step.
commonUseCases: Caching system prompt + tool schemas across every agent loop step
Reusing a large fixed document/context across many questions
Keeping few-shot examples in a stable cached prefix

commonMisconceptions.myth: Prompt caching caches the model's answers.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It caches the computed prefix (the model's internal representation of the input tokens), not the output. The model still generates a fresh response every call — caching only makes reading the repeated prefix cheaper and faster.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Message order doesn't matter as long as the content is present.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Caching matches on the leading tokens, so a cache hit requires the static content to come first and be byte-identical. A variable value (like a timestamp) placed early busts the cache on every call.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every provider caches the same way with no code changes.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Some providers cache long identical prefixes automatically, while others require an explicit cache_control breakpoint to opt in. The stable-prefix rule is universal, but whether you must mark the boundary depends on the provider.

interactiveExamples.title: Cost per step with and without caching
interactiveExamples.explanation: Compute an agent step's input cost when the static system+tools prefix is cached versus paid at full rate. The cached prefix is billed at roughly 10% of the normal input rate, so the saving grows with how big the reused prefix is.

code.code:
IN_RATE = 0.003        # full input rate per 1k tokens
CACHED_RATE = 0.0003   # ~10% of full for cached prefix tokens

def step_input_cost(prefix_tokens, fresh_tokens, cached: bool):
    if cached:
        return (prefix_tokens/1000)*CACHED_RATE + (fresh_tokens/1000)*IN_RATE
    return ((prefix_tokens + fresh_tokens)/1000)*IN_RATE

prefix, fresh = 4000, 500   # big static prefix, small fresh user turn
no_cache = step_input_cost(prefix, fresh, cached=False)
with_cache = step_input_cost(prefix, fresh, cached=True)

print("no cache:  ", round(no_cache, 5))
print("with cache:", round(with_cache, 5))
print("saving:    ", f"{(1 - with_cache/no_cache)*100:.0f}%")
code.caption: The 4000-token prefix drops from full rate to ~10%, so the step gets much cheaper; only the small fresh turn stays at full price.

interactiveExamples.title: Stable-prefix ordering across a full loop
interactiveExamples.explanation: Simulate an agent loop where the static system+tools prefix is sent every step. The first step misses (primes the cache) and later steps hit, while the fresh per-step content is always billed at full rate. This shows why prefix ordering plus repetition is where caching pays off.

code.code:
IN_RATE, CACHED_RATE = 0.003, 0.0003

def build(prefix_tokens, user_tokens):
    # static prefix FIRST, variable user turn LAST -> cacheable
    return {"prefix": prefix_tokens, "fresh": user_tokens}

def run_loop(steps, prefix_tokens, fresh_per_step):
    seen_prefix = False
    total = 0.0
    for i in range(steps):
        msg = build(prefix_tokens, fresh_per_step)
        if seen_prefix:                      # cache HIT on the prefix
            prefix_cost = (msg["prefix"]/1000)*CACHED_RATE
        else:                                # first step MISS, primes cache
            prefix_cost = (msg["prefix"]/1000)*IN_RATE
            seen_prefix = True
        fresh_cost = (msg["fresh"]/1000)*IN_RATE
        total += prefix_cost + fresh_cost
    return round(total, 5)

print("cached loop: ", run_loop(5, prefix_tokens=4000, fresh_per_step=500))
# compare to paying full prefix rate every step:
full = round(5 * ((4000+500)/1000)*IN_RATE, 5)
print("uncached loop:", full)
code.caption: Only step 1 pays full price for the prefix; steps 2-5 hit the cache, so the 5-step loop costs far less than paying full rate every time.

codeLab.title: Build a cache-friendly message builder and cost estimator
codeLab.instructions: Implement two functions. (1) build_messages(system: str, tools: str, user: str) -> list[dict] must return messages ordered so the STATIC content (system, then tools) comes first and the VARIABLE user turn comes last — this is what makes the prefix cacheable. (2) estimate_loop_cost(prefix_tokens, fresh_tokens, steps, in_rate, cached_rate) -> float must return the total input cost of an agent loop where the prefix is paid at full in_rate on the first step (cache miss) and at cached_rate on every subsequent step (cache hit), while the fresh tokens are always billed at in_rate. Round the result to 5 decimals. Complete both so the harness passes.
codeLab.testHarness:
msgs = build_messages("SYS", "TOOLS", "hello")
assert [m["role"] for m in msgs] == ["system", "system", "user"]
assert msgs[0]["content"] == "SYS" and msgs[-1]["content"] == "hello"

# 1 step: only the miss, no cache benefit yet
one = estimate_loop_cost(4000, 500, 1, 0.003, 0.0003)
assert one == round((4000/1000)*0.003 + (500/1000)*0.003, 5), one

# 5 steps: step 0 full prefix, steps 1-4 cached prefix
five = estimate_loop_cost(4000, 500, 5, 0.003, 0.0003)
expected = round((4000/1000)*0.003 + 4*(4000/1000)*0.0003 + 5*(500/1000)*0.003, 5)
assert five == expected, (five, expected)

# caching must be cheaper than paying full every step
full = round(5*((4000+500)/1000)*0.003, 5)
assert five < full
print("all tests passed")
hints: For build_messages, just return the list in the order system, tools, user — order is the whole point, since caching matches leading tokens.
In estimate_loop_cost, use the loop index: `rate = in_rate if i == 0 else cached_rate` captures 'first step misses, rest hit'.
Fresh tokens are never cached, so always price them at in_rate regardless of the step; round the final total to 5 decimals.

theory.question: What is prompt caching and why does it matter so much for agents specifically?
theory.directAnswer: Prompt caching stores the model's computed representation of a prompt prefix so a later call with the same leading tokens skips recomputation and bills those tokens at a steep discount. It matters most for agents because an agent loop re-sends the same system prompt and tool definitions on every iteration, and those repeated tokens dominate input cost — caching makes that large, unchanging prefix nearly free.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A provider feature that caches the precomputed key/value representation of a message prefix, keyed by its exact leading tokens, and reuses it on matching subsequent requests at a reduced rate.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Recomputing an identical multi-thousand-token prefix on every call is wasteful in both cost and latency; caching lets the model reuse that work instead of redoing it each time.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You order messages so all static content (system rules, tool schemas, fixed context) leads and all variable content trails. On the first call the prefix is computed and stored (a miss); matching later calls hit the cache and bill the prefix at the cached rate. Entries expire after a short idle window, and some providers require an explicit cache_control breakpoint while others cache automatically.

theory.whyImportant: It is one of the highest-leverage, lowest-risk cost optimizations for agents because it targets the most repetitive part of the workload — the re-sent system and tools — without changing model behavior or output quality.
theory.realWorldExample: A support agent with a 4,000-token system+tools prefix runs a 6-step loop per ticket; caching bills that prefix at ~10% on steps 2-6, cutting input cost by most of it and lowering time-to-first-token on every step.

followUps.question: Does caching change the model's output?
followUps.answer: No. It only reuses the computed input prefix to save cost and latency; the model still generates a fresh response each call, so quality is unaffected.

followUps.question: What invalidates a cached prefix?
followUps.answer: Any difference in the leading tokens — a changed word, an early timestamp, reordered content — plus expiry after the cache's idle window. That's why variable content must go last.

theory.question: How do you design a prompt to maximize cache hits, and how does this differ across providers?
theory.directAnswer: Order the request so every static element — system instructions, tool schemas, long fixed context, few-shot examples — comes first as a byte-identical prefix, and put everything variable (the user's turn, timestamps, retrieved snippets) at the end. On explicit-caching providers you also mark where the cacheable prefix ends with a cache_control breakpoint; on automatic-caching providers long identical prefixes are cached for you with no flag.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A message-ordering discipline (static-first, variable-last) combined with provider-specific opt-in mechanics for marking the cache boundary.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Caches match on leading tokens, so a hit is only possible when the prefix is identical across calls; anything that changes early breaks the match, and different providers expose different controls for where caching applies.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Concatenate immutable content at the front, keep it stable across calls, and avoid embedding volatile values (time, request IDs, random ordering) in the prefix. On Anthropic-style APIs you attach cache_control to the last message of the prefix to set the breakpoint; on OpenAI-style APIs caching of long identical prefixes is automatic, giving less control but no code change.

theory.whyImportant: Prefix design is the difference between caching helping on every step and never getting a hit; a single misplaced variable value can silently erase all the savings.
theory.realWorldExample: A team moved a per-request timestamp out of the system prompt into the user turn; hit rate jumped from near zero to almost every step, cutting the agent's input bill sharply with no behavior change.

followUps.question: Where should retrieved RAG context go for best caching?
followUps.answer: If it changes per query, put it after the static prefix so it doesn't bust the cache; if a large document is reused across many questions, place it in the cacheable prefix instead.

followUps.question: Why does the first call never hit?
followUps.answer: There is nothing stored yet — the first call computes and stores the prefix (a miss), and only subsequent matching calls within the expiry window hit.

scenario.question: Your agent's input bill is high and caching seems enabled, but the hit rate is near zero. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: Inspect the exact bytes of the prompt prefix across consecutive calls to find what changes early. The usual culprit is a volatile value (timestamp, request ID, randomized tool order, per-user data) placed inside the leading static content, which breaks the byte-identical match. Move all such variable content after the static prefix, keep the static block stable and ordered, and — on an explicit-caching provider — confirm the cache_control breakpoint is set on the right message. Then verify hit rate rises via provider usage metrics.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A cache-effectiveness debugging problem where the prefix is not stable enough to match across calls.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Caching is prefix-exact, so any early-varying token — even one injected accidentally by a template — prevents hits, and it often goes unnoticed because the agent still works, just expensively.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Log or diff the serialized prefix of two back-to-back requests, locate the first differing token, and trace it to its source (often string interpolation of time/IDs or non-deterministic dict/tool ordering). Refactor so the prefix is deterministic and static, relocate variable data to the suffix, and re-measure the cached-token ratio the provider reports.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows the practical failure mode of caching — it's silently ineffective rather than broken — and the metrics-driven, byte-level diagnosis needed to recover the savings.
scenario.realWorldExample: A diff of two prefixes revealed a `Session started: <iso timestamp>` line at the top of the system prompt; moving it into the user message raised the cached-token share from ~5% to over 90% and cut input cost dramatically.

followUps.question: How would you monitor cache effectiveness going forward?
followUps.answer: Track the provider-reported cached vs uncached input token counts as a hit-rate metric per agent, and alert if it drops, since a prompt change can silently reintroduce an early variable.

followUps.question: Could tool ordering break caching?
followUps.answer: Yes — if tool schemas are serialized in a non-deterministic order (e.g. from a set), the prefix bytes differ each call; sort them into a fixed order to keep the prefix stable.

coding.question: Write a function that estimates an agent loop's input cost with prompt caching, where the static prefix misses on the first step and hits on every later step, and returns both the cached and uncached totals for comparison.
coding.thoughtProcess: The prefix is billed at the full input rate exactly once (the priming miss on step 0) and at the cached rate on every subsequent step, while the fresh per-step tokens are always full rate. I iterate over steps, pick the prefix rate based on whether it's the first step, and accumulate. I compute the uncached baseline by pricing the whole prompt at full rate every step, then return both so the caller can see the saving. Rounding keeps the output stable.

solution.code:
def estimate_caching(prefix_tokens, fresh_tokens, steps,
                     in_rate=0.003, cached_rate=0.0003):
    cached_total = 0.0
    uncached_total = 0.0
    for i in range(steps):
        # first step primes the cache (miss = full rate); rest hit
        prefix_rate = in_rate if i == 0 else cached_rate
        cached_total += (prefix_tokens/1000)*prefix_rate + (fresh_tokens/1000)*in_rate
        # baseline: full rate for the whole prompt every step
        uncached_total += ((prefix_tokens + fresh_tokens)/1000)*in_rate
    return {
        "cached": round(cached_total, 5),
        "uncached": round(uncached_total, 5),
        "saving_pct": round((1 - cached_total/uncached_total)*100, 1),
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(estimate_caching(prefix_tokens=4000, fresh_tokens=500, steps=5))

lineByLine: The loop runs once per agent step, accumulating a cached and an uncached total in parallel for comparison.
prefix_rate is the full in_rate only on step 0 (the priming miss) and the discounted cached_rate on every later step (the hits).
cached_total prices the prefix at its per-step rate plus the fresh tokens, which are never cached and always full rate.
uncached_total is the baseline: the entire prompt (prefix + fresh) at full rate every step, as if caching were off.
The return dict reports both totals plus the percentage saved, so the caller can judge whether caching is worth the added request complexity.
The __main__ block runs a 5-step example showing the cached total, uncached baseline, and saving.
coding.timeComplexity: O(steps) — a single pass over the loop iterations.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — only running totals are kept.

followUps.question: How would you extend this to model cache expiry?
followUps.answer: Track the time since the last hit and treat a step as a miss (full prefix rate) whenever the idle gap exceeds the cache TTL, resetting the primed state.

followUps.question: How would growing history change the estimate?
followUps.answer: Only the stable prefix is cached; the growing conversation is fresh each step, so you'd increase fresh_tokens per step to reflect the accumulating history billed at full rate.

keyTakeaways: Prompt caching reuses the model's computed prefix (not its answer), billing repeated leading tokens at a steep discount and processing them faster.
Caches match on exact leading tokens, so order messages static-first, variable-last — one changed character early busts the whole prefix.
The first call is always a miss that primes the cache; later matching calls hit until the entry expires after a short idle window.
Providers differ: some require an explicit cache_control breakpoint, others cache long identical prefixes automatically — but the stable-prefix rule is universal.
Savings scale with the reused-prefix ratio, which is high in agent loops that re-send system+tools every step; prove it with a before/after cost calculation.
